paper.title: Current state of Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steels
paper.paper_scope: A critical review of the physical metallurgy, phase equilibria, processing strategies, strengthening and deformation mechanisms, and mechanical/application properties of Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density steels, which are classified into four families (ferritic Fe-Al, ferrite-based duplex, austenite-based duplex/triplex and austenitic) for potential automotive structural applications.

alloys.description: Ferritic low density steels based principally on the binary Fe-Al system; ferrite (disordered A2, ordered B2 FeAl or DO3 Fe3Al depending on Al content) is the matrix phase at hot working temperature.
alloys.alloys_notes: Ferritic Fe-Al low-density alloys can contain up to 5% Mn but only a very low amount of C (<0.03-0.05%); Al content commonly limited to 7% (max 9%) for automotive applications to avoid embrittlement from the A2 to K1/B2/DO3 transition.

source.reason: Table 2 classifies ferritic Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight steels with typical composition Al ~5-9%, Mn <5%, C <0.05%; block b0041 states ferritic Fe-Al low-density alloys contain up to 5% Mn and only a very low amount of C, with an elongated δ-ferrite microstructure.

alloys.alloy_name: Ferrite based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel
aliases: ferrite based duplex low density steels
alloys.description: Duplex low density steels with a δ-ferrite + austenite microstructure at hot working temperature, where the δ-ferrite fraction is larger than 50%; austenite stability is relatively low due to lower alloying contents.
alloys.alloys_notes: Low C (0.1-0.4%), medium Mn (3-9%) and medium Al (3-6%) contents; a bimodal microstructure of clustered austenite particles in a coarse-grained δ-ferrite matrix can be obtained through process control.

source.reason: Table 2 gives the typical composition range for ferrite based duplex low density steels as Al ~3-7%, Mn ~2-12%, C ~0.05-0.5%; block b0047 describes this family as having an α+δ-ferrite microstructure at hot working temperature with the δ-ferrite fraction larger than 50%.

alloys.alloy_name: Austenite based duplex Fe-Mn-Al-C low density steel
alloys.description: Duplex low density steels with an austenite + δ-ferrite microstructure at hot working temperature in which the austenitic phase forms the continuous matrix; at the final stage they contain small amounts of δ-ferrite and intragranular nano-sized κ-carbides in an austenite matrix (hence also called Triplex steels).
alloys.alloys_notes: δ-ferrite content typically below ~10-30%; Al content above 7% promotes ordered B2/DO3 domains in ferrite, so an upper Al limit of 7% is specified for duplex steels.

source.reason: Table 2 gives the typical composition range for austenite based duplex low density steels as Al ~5-10%, Mn ~5-30%, C ~0.4-0.7%; block b0048 describes this family as γ+δ at hot working temperature with an austenitic continuous matrix and states they are also called Triplex steels.

alloys.description: Austenitic low density steels with a fully equiaxed austenitic microstructure at hot working temperature; the austenite is metastable after fast cooling and is the most promising class in terms of properties and processing.
alloys.alloys_notes: Typical compositions for austenitic low-density steels are 15-30% Mn, 7-10% Al and 0.7-1.2% C with the balance Fe; κ-carbide precipitation hardening requires Al >7% and C >0.7%.

source.reason: Table 2 gives the typical composition range for austenitic low density steels as Al ~5-12%, Mn ~12-30%, C ~0.6-2.0%; block b0046 states austenitic low density steels contain higher Mn (12-30%), Al up to 12% and C 0.6-2.0% with a fully equiaxed austenitic microstructure.

processes.process_name: Cold rolled and recrystallization annealed ferritic Fe-Al steel
processes.description: Ferritic Fe-Al steels are cold rolled and then recrystallization annealed at 700-1000°C to control the ferrite grain size and texture as well as the precipitation of κ-carbides; a fully recrystallized microstructure is obtained after annealing in 700-950°C following ~50% cold reduction.
processes.processes_notes: Hot rolling alone cannot refine the δ-ferrite so cold rolling plus annealing is necessary for ferritic low density steels.

source.reason: Block b0105 states ferritic Fe-Al steels are generally cold rolled and heated to 700-1000°C for recrystallization annealing to control grain size/texture and κ-carbide precipitation; block b0114 describes cold rolling and annealing (700-950°C) to obtain recrystallized microstructures.

processes.process_name: Cold rolled, intercritically annealed and austempered ferrite based duplex steel
processes.description: Cold rolled ferrite based duplex steels are annealed at an intercritical temperature of 700-900°C, followed by an austempering (isothermal bainitic) treatment, to refine the δ-ferrite and γ phases and adjust austenite stability/morphology and retain austenite at room temperature.
processes.processes_notes: A variant anneals at 780-980°C for 50 s then fast cools (15°C/s) to 400°C and austempers at 400°C for 180 s.

source.reason: Block b0105 states ferrite based duplex steels are cold rolled and then annealed at an intercritical temperature from 700 to 900°C, followed by austempering; block b0164 details intercritical annealing plus austempering for a Fe-3.5Mn-5.8Al-0.35C alloy.

processes.process_name: Solution treated and water quenched austenite based duplex steel
processes.description: Austenite based duplex steels are solution treated in the temperature range ~900-1100°C and then water quenched, giving a γ + δ-ferrite (and possibly nano-sized κ') microstructure; e.g. Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C solution treated at 1050°C and water quenched.
processes.processes_notes: Fast cooling/water quenching avoids formation of coarse intergranular κ-carbides.

source.reason: Block b0195 describes a Fe-27Mn-11.5Al-0.95C duplex steel after solution treatment at 1050°C and water quenching; block b0194 describes triplex steels in the solution treated and water quenched condition; Table 4 (b0206) gives SIP alloy solution treatment 1050°C/25 min + water quenching.

processes.process_name: Solution treated and water quenched austenitic steel
processes.description: Austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels are solution treated in the temperature range ~900-1100°C and then water quenched to produce a single austenite phase with SROs or uniformly distributed nano-sized κ'-carbides, avoiding coarse intergranular κ-carbide/α particles.
processes.processes_notes: Fast cooling (water quenching) from solution treatment temperatures is used to avoid coarse κ-carbide and/or α-particle formation.

source.reason: Block b0107 states age-hardenable austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C cold rolled strips are solution treated at 900-1100°C and then quenched in water/oil; block b0118 states austenitic steels are usually fast cooled (water quenched) from solution treatment temperatures ~900-1100°C; block b0230 reports solution treatment of Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl series.

processes.process_name: Solution treated and aged austenitic steel
processes.description: Age-hardenable austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels are held isothermally for 5-20 h in the temperature range 500-700°C after solution treatment and quenching, producing precipitation hardening through homogeneous intragranular κ'-carbide precipitation.
processes.processes_notes: Common practice is 550°C for ~16-24 h; peak strength increases and aging kinetics accelerate as C content increases. Age hardening is not a necessary step for automotive applications but may occur as a consequence of overaging in continuous annealing lines.

source.reason: Block b0107 states the common practice for age hardening is to hold isothermally for 5-20 h in the temperature range 500-700°C (processes 4 and 5); block b0241-0242 describe the effect of aging at 550°C for 24 h and 16 h on tensile properties; block b0255 discusses short aging / controlled cooling producing κ-carbides.

processes.process_name: Cold rolled and annealed non-age hardenable austenitic steel
processes.description: For non-age hardenable austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels, after cold rolling, recovery or recrystallization annealing in the temperature range 600-900°C for a short time (1-5 min) is applied to restore ductility or obtain grain refinement via continuous annealing.
processes.processes_notes: After cold rolling, annealing in 500-1000°C above the M7C3 formation temperature can be applied to partially recover ductility or yield fine recrystallized austenitic grains.

source.reason: Block b0107 states that for non-age hardenable austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels, after cold rolling, recovery or recrystallization annealing at 600-900°C for 1-5 min restores ductility or refines grains; block b0258 describes combining cold rolling with annealing in 500-1000°C for non-age hardenable austenitic steels (Al<7%).

unmapped_findings: The addition of Al to Fe-C steels gives a 1.3% reduction in density and a ~2-2.5% reduction in Young's modulus per 1 wt% Al addition.

Fe-Mn-Al-C lightweight alloys are classified into four categories (ferritic, ferrite based duplex, austenite based duplex and austenitic steels) according to the matrix phase at high (hot working) temperature, assuming near-equilibrium conditions.
κ-carbide precipitation is a unique strengthening mechanism in austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steels bearing high amounts of Al and C; intragranular κ'-carbide requires Al >7% and C >0.7%.

New deformation mechanisms (MBIP, DSBR, SIP) in addition to TRIP/TWIP describe plastic deformation of high-SFE Fe-Mn-Al-C austenitic steels; examples: SIP Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.9C, MBIP Fe-28Mn-10Al-1.0C, DSBR Fe-30.4Mn-8Al-1.2C.

The corrosion resistance of Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is not improved relative to conventional high strength steels, and application properties such as fatigue, formability, weldability and coatability are not well documented.
